changes.before: Hvor er jeg glad for at være rejst! Kære ven, hvor er menneskehjertet dog en sælsom ting! At forlade dig, som jeg har været uadskillelig fra, som jeg elsker så højt, og dog at føle mig lykkelig! Jeg ved, du tilgiver mig. Var mine øvrige bindinger ikke ligefrem udvalgt af skæbnen til at pine et sind som mit? Stakkels Leonora! Og dog var jeg uden skyld. Var det min skyld, at der, mens hendes søsters særlige ynder gav mig så behagelig en underholdning, slog en lidenskab rod i hendes eget skrøbelige hjerte? Og dog — er jeg helt uskyldig? Opmuntrede jeg ikke hendes følelser? Frydede jeg mig ikke over de ægte naturudtryk, der, skønt de næppe var morsomme i sig selv, så ofte fik os til at le? Gjorde jeg ikke — åh, hvad er dog et menneske, at det tør anklage sig selv sådan? Jeg lover dig, kære ven, jeg vil blive bedre; jeg vil ikke længere tygge drøv på hver lille fortrædelighed, skæbnen deler ud, sådan som jeg altid har gjort; jeg vil nyde det nærværende, og lade det forbigangne være forbi. Du har ret, min bedste ven — der ville være langt mindre lidelse blandt os, hvis menneskene ikke arbejdede så ihærdigt med deres indbildningskraft på at kalde mindet om gammel sorg tilbage, i stedet for at bære det nærværende med nogen sindsro — Gud ved hvorfor vi er skabt sådan. Vær så venlig at sige til min mor, at jeg vil tage mig af hendes sag, så godt jeg kan, og sende hende besked om det snarest muligt. Jeg har set min tante, og hun er slet ikke den ubehagelige kvinde, vore slægtninge gør hende til. Hun er livlig og varm, med det venligste hjerte. Jeg forklarede min mors klage over den del af hendes arv, der er blevet holdt tilbage. Min tante fortalte mig sine egne grunde og bevæggrunde, og på hvilke vilkår hun er villig til at give det hele fra sig — og gøre mere, end vi bad om. Jeg kan ikke skrive mere om det lige nu; forsikr blot min mor om, at det hele nok skal gå. Og endnu en gang, kære ven, har denne lille sag vist mig, at misforståelse og forsømmelse volder mere ufred i verden end selv ondskab og grusomhed. I det mindste er de to sidste sjældnere.
changes.after: Hvor er jeg glad for at være rejst! Min kære ven, hvor er menneskets hjerte dog mærkeligt! At forlade dig, som jeg har været uadskillelig fra, og som jeg elsker så højt, og alligevel være glad! Jeg ved, at du vil tilgive mig. Har skæbnen ikke netop givet mig andre forbindelser for at plage et hjerte som mit? Stakkels Leonora! Og dog var det ikke min skyld. Kunne jeg gøre for, at hun forelskede sig i mig med sit skrøbelige hjerte, mens jeg nød hendes søsters særlige charme? Men er jeg helt uden skyld? Opmuntrede jeg ikke hendes følelser? Blev jeg ikke betaget af de ægte, umiddelbare udtryk for hendes natur, som så ofte morede os, selv om de egentlig ikke var særlig morsomme? Gjorde jeg ikke — men åh, hvad er et menneske, at det tør anklage sig selv sådan? Kære ven, jeg lover dig, at jeg vil forbedre mig. Jeg vil ikke længere, som jeg altid har gjort, gruble over hver lille modgang, skæbnen sender mig. Jeg vil nyde nutiden og lade fortiden være fortid. Du har uden tvivl ret, min bedste ven: Der ville være langt mindre lidelse blandt mennesker, hvis vi ikke brugte fantasien så flittigt på at genkalde os gammel sorg i stedet for at bære vores nuværende lod med sindsro. Gud ved, hvorfor vi er sådan. Sig til min mor, at jeg vil tage mig af hendes sag, så godt jeg kan, og give hende besked så hurtigt som muligt. Jeg har besøgt min tante. Hun er langt fra så ubehagelig, som vores venner påstår. Hun er en livlig, glad kvinde med det bedste hjerte. Jeg forklarede hende, hvordan min mor var blevet uretfærdigt behandlet ved at få en del af sin arv holdt tilbage. Hun forklarede sine egne grunde og de vilkår, hun er villig til at afgive det hele på og endda gøre mere, end vi har bedt om. Jeg kan ikke skrive mere om den sag nu. Forsikr blot min mor om, at det nok skal gå godt. Igen har jeg i denne lille sag set, kære ven, at misforståelser og forsømmelse gør mere skade i verden end selv ond vilje og ondskab. De to sidste forekommer i hvert fald sjældnere.

changes.before: Ellers har jeg det meget godt her. Ensomheden i dette jordiske paradis er en lindrende balsam for mit sind, og dette unge forår varmer mit ofte ængstelige hjerte med al sin gavmilde forjættelse. Hvert træ, hver busk er én eneste blomstermasse; man kunne ønske sig at være en sommerfugl, fri til at svæve omkring i dette ocean af duft og finde hele sit liv i det.
changes.after: Ellers har jeg det rigtig godt her. Ensomheden i dette jordiske paradis er en behagelig balsam for mit sind. Det unge forår glæder mit ofte ængstelige hjerte med sine rige løfter. Hvert træ og hver busk er fuld af blomster. Man kunne ønske at blive forvandlet til en oldenborre, svæve omkring i dette hav af duft og finde al sin næring i det.
changes.reason: Modern Danish, additionally crosschecked against Goethe's German primary text. German-confirmed details take precedence over Boylan intermediate translation; retain original meaning and imagery.

changes.before: Selve byen er ubehagelig, men rundt om den ligger en ubeskrivelig naturskønhed. Det var det, der fik den afdøde grev M til at anlægge en have på en af de skrånende høje, der krydser hinanden her i den dejligste afveksling og danner de mest yndige dale. Haven er enkel, og i det øjeblik man træder ind, mærker man, at den ikke er tegnet af en uddannet gartner, men af en mand, der ville have et sted, hvor han kunne hengive sig til sit eget følende hjerte. Jeg har allerede fældet mangen en tåre for dens døde herre i et lysthus, der nu er ved at forfalde — hans yndlingsplet, og nu min. Snart er jeg selv herre over stedet. Gartneren er blevet glad for mig i de sidste par dage, og han kommer ikke til at lide under det.
changes.after: Selve byen er ubehagelig, men rundt om den er naturen ubeskriveligt smuk. Derfor anlagde den afdøde grev M en have på en af de skråninger, der her mødes i den dejligste afveksling og danner smukke dale. Haven er enkel. Allerede ved første besøg mærker man, at den ikke er planlagt af en faguddannet gartner, men af en mand, som her ville give sig hen til sit følsomme hjertes glæder. Jeg har allerede fældet mange tårer til minde om den døde ejer i et lysthus, der nu ligger i ruiner. Det var hans yndlingssted, og nu er det mit. Snart vil jeg være herre over stedet. Gartneren er blevet glad for mig i løbet af de sidste dage, og det skal han ikke komme til at fortryde.
changes.reason: Modern Danish preserving introspective repetitions; restore friends not relatives, cheerful not warm, and already ruined summer-house.

changes.before: En vidunderlig ro har taget min hele sjæl i besiddelse, ligesom disse søde forårsmorgener, som jeg nyder af hele mit hjerte. Jeg er alene og glad for at være i live på dette sted, der blev skabt for sjæle som min. Jeg er så lykkelig, kære ven, så fortabt i den rene fornemmelse af stille tilværelse, at min kunst lider under det. Jeg kunne ikke tegne en eneste streg lige nu — og dog har jeg aldrig været en større maler, end jeg er i dette øjeblik. Når den dejlige dal damper af tåge omkring mig, og den høje middagssol hviler på overfladen af mine træers tætte løvtag, mens kun nogle få strejfende stråler smutter ind i det indre helligdom, og jeg lægger mig i det høje græs ved den rislende bæk — da, tæt ved jorden, lægger jeg mærke til tusind små planter, jeg aldrig havde set; når jeg hører summen af den lille verden mellem stænglerne og bliver fortrolig med de utallige sælsomme former af insekterne og fluerne, da føler jeg den Almægtiges nærvær, han som skabte os i sit eget billede, åndedraget af den altomfavnende kærlighed, der bærer og holder os, mens den svæver omkring os i en evighed af lyksalighed. Min ven! Når lyset så svigter i mine øjne, og verden omkring mig og himlen ovenover kommer helt til hvile i min sjæl som ansigtet på en kvinde, jeg elsker, gribes jeg ofte af længsel og tænker: åh, kunne jeg blot udtrykke dette, kunne ånde alt det, der lever så fuldt og varmt i mig, ned på papiret, så det kunne spejle min sjæl, som min sjæl spejler den uendelige Gud! Min ven — men det overgår mine kræfter; jeg går under, knust af disse syners blotte vælde.
changes.after: En vidunderlig ro har fyldt hele min sjæl, ligesom disse dejlige forårsmorgener, som jeg nyder af hele mit hjerte. Jeg er alene og mærker glæden ved at være til på dette sted, der synes skabt til at gøre sjæle som min lykkelige. Jeg er så glad, min kære ven, så opslugt af den fine fornemmelse af blot at eksistere i fred, at min kunst lider under det. Lige nu kunne jeg ikke tegne en eneste streg, og alligevel føler jeg, at jeg aldrig har været en større maler end nu. Når den smukke dal fyldes af dis omkring mig, og middagssolen rammer oversiden af træernes tætte løvtag, mens kun enkelte stråler slipper ind i den inderste helligdom, kaster jeg mig ned i det høje græs ved den rislende bæk. Tæt ved jorden opdager jeg tusind ukendte planter. Jeg hører den lille verden summe mellem stænglerne og bliver fortrolig med insekternes og fluernes utallige, ubeskrivelige former. Så mærker jeg nærværet af den Almægtige, der skabte os i sit billede, og åndedraget fra den altomfattende kærlighed, som bærer og opretholder os og svæver omkring os i evig lykke. Og når det så mørkner for mine øjne, min ven, og himmel og jord synes at bo i min sjæl ligesom billedet af en elsket kvinde, tænker jeg ofte længselsfuldt: Åh, kunne jeg bare beskrive disse indtryk! Kunne jeg fæstne alt det på papiret, som lever så fuldt og varmt i mig, så det blev et spejl af min sjæl, ligesom min sjæl er et spejl af den uendelige Gud! Åh, min ven, det overstiger mine kræfter. Jeg synker sammen under vægten af disse strålende syn!
changes.reason: Modern Danish, additionally crosschecked against Goethe's German primary text. German-confirmed details take precedence over Boylan intermediate translation; retain original meaning and imagery.

changes.before: Jeg kan ikke afgøre, om bedrageriske ånder svæver over dette sted, eller om det er den varme, himmelske indbildningskraft i mit eget hjerte, der forvandler alt omkring mig til paradis. Lige foran huset er der en kilde — en kilde, der holder mig i sin trolddom, som Melusine og hendes søstre. Man går ned ad en blid skråning og kommer til en hvælving, og en tyve trin længere nede vælder det klareste krystalvand frem af marmorklippen. Den lave mur, der indhegner den foroven, de høje træer, der omkranser stedet, selve stedets kølighed — det hele gør et indtryk, der på én gang er behageligt og højtideligt. Der går ikke en dag, hvor jeg ikke tilbringer en time der. De unge piger kommer ud fra byen for at hente vand — uskyldigt, nødvendigt arbejde, som engang selv kongedøtre udførte. Når jeg sidder og hviler der, vågner det gamle patriarkalske liv til live omkring mig: jeg ser dem, vore forfædre, slutte venskaber og indgå ægteskaber ved brønden, og jeg fornemmer, hvordan venlige ånder vågede over kilderne og strømmene. Den, der ikke kan dele disse følelser, har aldrig rigtig kendt den lindring, det er at hvile ved køligt vand efter en hård sommerdag.
changes.after: Jeg ved ikke, om der færdes ånder her, som narrer mig, eller om det er den varme, himmelske fantasi i mit eget hjerte, der får alt omkring mig til at ligne et paradis. Lige uden for byen ligger en kilde, som jeg er bundet til af en fortryllelse, ligesom Melusine og hendes søstre. Går man ned ad en let skrånende sti, kommer man til en hvælving. Omtrent tyve trin længere nede strømmer krystalklart vand frem af marmorklippen. Den smalle mur, som omgiver kilden foroven, de høje træer omkring stedet og selve køligheden — alt gør et behageligt og samtidig ophøjet indtryk. Der går ikke en dag, uden at jeg tilbringer en time der. De unge piger kommer fra byen for at hente vand. Et uskyldigt og nødvendigt arbejde, som engang blev udført af kongedøtre. Når jeg hviler der, vækkes billedet af de gamle patriarkers liv omkring mig. Jeg ser vores forfædre lære hinanden at kende og fri ved kilden, og jeg mærker, hvordan gode ånder vogtede over kilder og vandløb. Den, der ikke kender disse følelser, har aldrig virkelig nydt at hvile i køligheden ved en kilde efter en trættende sommerdag.
changes.reason: Modern Danish, additionally crosschecked against Goethe's German primary text. German-confirmed details take precedence over Boylan intermediate translation; retain original meaning and imagery.

changes.before: Du spørger, om du skal sende mig bøger. Kære ven, for Guds skyld, skån mig for det åg! Jeg vil ikke længere vejledes, ophidses, opildnes — mit hjerte syder rigeligt af sig selv. Hvad jeg trænger til, er noget at dysse mig i søvn med, og det finder jeg fuldkomment i min Homer. Hvor ofte forsøger jeg ikke at dæmpe feberen i mit blod; du har aldrig set noget så foranderligt, så ustadigt, som dette mit hjerte. Men det behøver jeg næppe at tilstå over for dig, som så ofte har måttet se mig svinge fra sorg til vild glæde, fra sødt tungsind til voldsom lidenskab. Jeg behandler mit stakkels hjerte som et sygt barn og lader det få, hvad det vil. Sig det ikke videre — der findes folk, der ville bebrejde mig det.
changes.after: Du spørger, om du skal sende mig bøger. Kære ven, jeg beder dig, for Guds skyld: Befri mig for det åg! Jeg behøver ikke mere, der vejleder mig, ryster mig eller ophidser mig. Mit hjerte gærer rigeligt af sig selv. Jeg trænger til toner, der kan berolige mig, og dem finder jeg fuldkomment hos min Homer. Jeg prøver ofte at dæmpe den brændende feber i mit blod. Du har aldrig set noget så ustadigt, så usikkert som mit hjerte. Men behøver jeg at tilstå det over for dig, min kære ven? Du har så ofte måttet lide ved at se mine pludselige skift fra sorg til voldsom glæde og fra mildt tungsind til heftige lidenskaber. Jeg behandler mit stakkels hjerte som et sygt barn og opfylder alle dets ønsker. Sig det ikke videre. Nogle ville bebrejde mig det.
changes.reason: Natural modern literary Danish preserving imagery and omitted emotional detail; restore soul's exhausted powers and soul/music metaphor.

changes.before: Almuen her kender mig allerede og holder af mig — især børnene. Da jeg først tilbragte tid med dem og venligt spurgte til deres små anliggender, troede nogle af dem, at jeg gjorde nar, og vendte sig fra mig i ægte fortrydelse. Jeg lod det ikke gå mig på; jeg følte blot, skarpere end nogensinde, noget jeg ofte har bemærket før. Folk, der kan gøre krav på en vis rang, holder sig køligt på afstand af almuen, som om de frygtede at miste deres værdighed ved berøringen, mens letsindige lediggængere og den slags, der holder af en ond spøg, lader, som om de nedlader sig til deres niveau, blot for at lade de fattige mærke deres frækhed des skarpere.
changes.after: De almindelige mennesker her kender mig allerede og holder af mig, især børnene. Da jeg først begyndte at færdes blandt dem og venligt spurgte til deres små anliggender, troede nogle, at jeg ville gøre nar af dem, og vendte mig ryggen i stor vrede. Det lod jeg mig ikke gå på. Jeg mærkede blot stærkere end før noget, jeg ofte har lagt mærke til: Folk med en vis rang holder sig køligt på afstand af almindelige mennesker, som om de frygter at miste deres betydning ved at komme tæt på dem. Samtidig lader letsindige lediggængere og folk med hang til grove spøgefuldheder, som om de stiger ned på de fattiges niveau, kun for at lade dem mærke deres uforskammethed desto stærkere.

changes.before: Jeg ved udmærket, at vi ikke alle er lige, og ikke kan være det. Men det er min mening, at en mand, der holder afstand til almuen for ikke at miste dens respekt, er lige så meget at dadle som en kujon, der gemmer sig for sin fjende af frygt for at tabe.
changes.after: Jeg ved godt, at vi ikke alle er lige og heller ikke kan være det. Men jeg mener, at den, der undgår almindelige mennesker for ikke at miste deres respekt, fortjener lige så megen kritik som en kujon, der gemmer sig for sin fjende af frygt for at tabe.

changes.before: Forleden gik jeg ned til kilden og fandt en ung tjenestepige, der havde sat sin krukke på det nederste trin og så sig om for at se, om en af hendes veninder kom for at hjælpe den op på hovedet. Jeg gik ned og så på hende. »Skal jeg hjælpe Dem, min kære?« sagde jeg. Hun blev blussende rød. »Åh nej, herre!« sagde hun. »Ingen ceremonier,« svarede jeg. Hun rettede puden på hovedet til rette, og jeg hjalp hende. Hun takkede mig og steg op ad trinnene.
changes.after: Forleden gik jeg ned til kilden. Der stod en ung tjenestepige, som havde sat sin krukke på det nederste trin og så sig om efter en af sine veninder, der kunne hjælpe hende med at løfte den op på hovedet. Jeg gik ned og så på hende. »Skal jeg hjælpe Dem, frøken?« spurgte jeg. Hun rødmede kraftigt. »Åh nej, min herre!« udbrød hun. »Ingen formaliteter!« svarede jeg. Hun rettede på sin krave, og jeg hjalp hende. Hun takkede mig og gik op ad trappen.

changes.before: Jeg har stiftet alle mulige bekendtskaber, men endnu ikke fundet noget egentligt samvær. Jeg ved ikke, hvad det er ved mig, der drager folk; så mange af dem fatter godhed for mig og knytter sig til mig, og det smerter mig, når vore veje kun følges et lille stykke. Spørger du, hvordan folk er her, må jeg svare: som alle vegne. Menneskeslægten er en ensformig affære. De fleste bruger størstedelen af deres liv på at arbejde blot for at holde sig i live, og den smule frihed, der bliver tilovers, skræmmer dem så meget, at de gør hvad som helst for at slippe af med den. Åh, menneskets lod!
changes.after: Jeg har fået alle mulige bekendte, men har endnu ikke fundet nogen, jeg rigtig føler mig hjemme hos. Jeg ved ikke, hvad der tiltrækker folk ved mig. Så mange kan lide mig og knytter sig til mig, og så bliver jeg ked af det, når vores fælles vej kun varer et kort stykke. Spørger du, hvordan mennesker er her, må jeg svare: »Som alle andre steder.« Menneskeslægten er en ensformig størrelse. De fleste arbejder det meste af tiden bare for at kunne leve. Den smule frihed, der bliver tilbage, gør dem så urolige, at de gør alt for at slippe af med den. Åh, menneskets skæbne!
changes.reason: Modern Danish with full class attitudes and narrator's possessive judgments retained; correct invented refusal and head cushion, restore running and praise of eldest daughter.

changes.before: Men de er en grundigt god slags. Når jeg en gang imellem slipper mig løs og deler de enkle glæder, der endnu er almuen forundt — sætter mig f.eks. med ægte åbenhed og godt humør ved et veldækket bord, eller får arrangeret en køretur eller en dans i rette øjeblik, og så videre — gør det mig usigelig godt; jeg må blot ikke huske på, at der ligger så mange andre kræfter ubrugte i mig, rådnende uden nytte, som jeg er nødt til at holde omhyggeligt skjult. Ak, den tanke vrider mit hjerte. Og dog er det vores lod, sådan nogen som os, at blive misforstået.
changes.after: Men det er virkelig gode mennesker. Når jeg af og til glemmer mig selv og deltager i de uskyldige glæder, som mennesker endnu har lov at nyde, gør det mig godt. For eksempel når jeg morer mig med ægte åbenhed og oprigtighed ved et veldækket bord eller på et passende tidspunkt arrangerer en udflugt eller en dans. Jeg må bare ikke tænke på alle de andre evner, som ligger i dvale i mig og rådner ubrugte op, og som jeg må holde omhyggeligt skjult. Åh, den tanke gør mig frygtelig nedtrykt. Men sådan nogen som os er nu engang dømt til at blive misforstået.
changes.reason: Modern Danish, additionally crosschecked against Goethe's German primary text. German-confirmed details take precedence over Boylan intermediate translation; retain original meaning and imagery.

changes.before: Hvor er det sørgeligt, at min ungdoms veninde er borte; hvor er det sørgeligt, at jeg nogensinde kendte hende! Jeg kunne sige til mig selv: du er en tåbe at lede efter, hvad der ikke står at finde her på jorden. Men hun var min. Jeg holdt det hjerte, den ædle sjæl, og i hendes nærvær syntes jeg at være mere, end jeg var, fordi jeg var alt, hvad jeg kunne være. Gode Gud — var en eneste af min sjæls kræfter da ladt ubrugt? Kunne jeg ikke for hende udfolde hele den hemmelighedsfulde følelse, hvormed mit hjerte favner naturen? Var vort samvær ikke en uendelig væv af den fineste følelse og den skarpeste vid, hvis hver mindste afvigelse, selv i sit mest spøgefulde, bar geniets stempel? Og nu — de få år, hun havde forud for mig, bar hende i graven før mig. Aldrig glemmer jeg hendes faste sind, hendes himmelske tålmod.
changes.after: Åh, at min ungdoms veninde er borte! Åh, at jeg nogensinde lærte hende at kende! Jeg kunne sige til mig selv: »Du er en drømmer, der søger noget, som ikke findes her på jorden.« Men hun har været min. Jeg har mærket det hjerte, den ædle sjæl, i hvis nærvær jeg syntes at være mere, end jeg var, fordi jeg var alt det, jeg kunne være. Gode Gud! Jeg sidder ofte i frugttræerne i Charlottes have med frugtplukkeren, den lange stang, og henter pærerne ned fra toppen. Hun står nedenunder og tager dem af, når jeg sænker dem ned til hende.

englishChanges.before: I can't tell whether deceiving spirits hover over this place, or whether it is the warm, heavenly imagination in my own heart that turns everything around me into paradise. Just in front of the house there is a spring — a spring that holds me under a spell, like Melusina and her sisters. You go down a gentle slope and come to an archway, and some twenty steps further down the clearest crystal water gushes from the marble rock. The low wall that encloses it at the top, the tall trees that ring the spot, the coolness of the place itself — it all makes an impression at once pleasant and solemn. Not a day goes by that I don't spend an hour there. The young girls come out from town to fetch water — innocent, necessary work that once even kings' daughters did. When I sit and rest there, the old patriarchal life comes alive around me: I can see them, our forefathers, striking up friendships and arranging matches at the well, and I feel how kindly spirits watched over the springs and streams. Anyone who can't share these feelings has never really known the relief of resting by cool water after a hard summer's day.

englishChanges.before: About a league from the town there is a place called Walheim. (The reader needn't bother looking for the place under that name; we have had to change the real names given in the original.) It sits beautifully on the side of a hill, and if you follow one of the footpaths out of the village, you get a view of the whole valley. A good old woman lives there and keeps a little inn; she sells wine, beer, and coffee, and for all her age she is cheerful and pleasant. The real charm of the place is two linden trees that spread their huge branches over the small green in front of the church, which is ringed all around by peasants' cottages, barns, and farmyards. I have rarely seen anywhere so quiet and out of the way, and I often have my table and chair brought out from the inn and drink my coffee there and read my Homer. I happened on the spot one fine afternoon and found it completely deserted; everyone was out in the fields except a little boy of about four, who was sitting on the ground holding a baby of about six months between his knees, pressing it to his chest with both arms so that they made a kind of armchair. For all the liveliness sparkling in its dark eyes, the baby sat perfectly still. The sight charmed me. I sat down on a plough opposite and sketched this little picture of brotherly tenderness with real delight. I added the hedge nearby, the barn door, and a few broken cartwheels, just as they lay; and after about an hour I found I had made a well-composed, interesting drawing without putting in anything of my own. That confirmed me in my resolve to keep, from now on, entirely to nature. Nature alone is inexhaustible, and nature alone forms great masters. You can say a great deal in favor of rules — much the same as can be said for the conventions of society: a man trained on them will never produce anything downright bad or offensive, just as a man who keeps the law and minds his manners can never be an utterly unbearable neighbor or an outright villain. But say what you like, rules destroy the true feeling of nature and the true expression of it. You'll tell me that's too severe — that rules only restrain, only prune away rank growth, and so on. My good friend, let me give you an analogy. It is just like love. A warm-hearted young man gives himself wholly to a girl, spends every hour of the day with her, wears out his health and pours out his money to prove again and again that he is utterly devoted to her. Then along comes some man of the world, some man of office and standing, and says to him: "My dear young fellow, love is natural — but you must love within limits. Divide up your time: give part of it to your work and save your free hours for your sweetheart. Reckon up your money, and from whatever is left over you may make her a present — only not too often: on her birthday, say, and the like." If the young man takes this advice, he'll make a useful member of society, and I'd urge any prince to give him a post — but it's all over with his love, and, if he's an artist, with his art. Oh, my friend! Why is it that the torrent of genius so seldom breaks loose, so seldom comes roaring down in a full flood to shake your astonished soul? Because along both banks of the stream live cool, respectable people whose summer-houses and tulip beds would be ruined by it, and who therefore dig their channels and throw up their dikes in good time to head off the danger.

englishChanges.before: I see I have fallen into raptures and grand talk and similes, and so forgotten to tell you what became of the children. Wrapped up in my artistic musings, which I sketched out for you yesterday, I went on sitting on that plough for a good two hours. Toward evening a young woman came hurrying toward the children, who hadn't stirred the whole time, with a basket on her arm, calling out from a distance, "Philip, you've been such a good boy!" She greeted me; I returned it, got up, and went over. I asked whether she was the mother of these pretty children. "Yes," she said, and giving the older one a piece of bread, she picked up the baby and kissed it with all a mother's tenderness. "I left my little one in Philip's care," she said, "while I went into town with my eldest to buy some white bread and sugar and an earthenware pot." I could see all of it in the basket, the lid having slipped off. "I want to make some broth tonight for my little Hans" — the baby — "but that wild one, the eldest, smashed my pot yesterday squabbling with Philip over the scrapings." I asked after the eldest, and she had barely told me he was driving a couple of geese home from the meadow when he came running up and handed Philip a willow switch. I talked with the woman a while longer and learned that she was the schoolmaster's daughter, and that her husband had gone off to Switzerland to collect a legacy left him by a relative. "They tried to cheat him out of it," she said, "and wouldn't answer his letters, so he's gone there himself. I only hope nothing has happened to him; I've heard nothing since he left." I found it hard to leave the woman; I gave each of the children a kreutzer, and one more for the baby, so she could bring it some white bread for its broth next time she went to town, and we parted. I tell you, dear friend, when my thoughts are all in an uproar, the sight of a creature like this settles my troubled mind. She moves contentedly, without a care, around the small circle of her life, getting through one day at a time; and when she sees the leaves fall it means nothing to her but that winter is coming. Since then I've gone out there often. The children have grown quite used to me; they get sugar when I drink my coffee, and in the evening they share my bread and butter and milk. On Sundays they always get their kreutzer, for the good woman has orders to hand it to them when I'm not there after the evening service. They're entirely at ease with me and tell me everything, and I get special pleasure from watching their little tempers and the simplicity of their ways when a few of the other village children are gathered with them.

englishChanges.before: I mentioned the other day that I'd got to know S—, the district steward, and that he'd invited me out to see him in his retreat — his little kingdom, rather. I put it off, and might never have gone if chance hadn't shown me the treasure hidden away in that quiet spot. Some of our young people had got up a country ball, and I agreed to go. I offered to escort a pretty, pleasant, but rather ordinary girl from the neighborhood, and it was settled that I'd hire a carriage and drive out with my partner and her aunt to collect Charlotte on the way. "You'll meet a very lovely young woman," my companion told me as we drove through the woods toward the hunting lodge. "Take care you don't lose your heart," the aunt added. "Why?" I asked. "Because she's already promised to a very fine man," she said, "who's away just now settling his affairs after his father's death, and stands to come into a sizable inheritance." The news meant nothing to me. As we reached the gate the sun was just going down behind the mountaintops. The air was heavy, and the ladies fretted about a storm coming on, with banks of low black cloud massing on the horizon. I soothed them by playing the weather prophet, though I had my own misgivings that our evening might be spoiled.

englishChanges.before: I got down, and a maid came to the door and asked us to wait a moment for her mistress. I crossed the courtyard to the handsome house, went up the front steps, and as I opened the door I saw the most charming sight I have ever laid eyes on. Six children, from eleven years old down to two, were rushing about the hall around a girl of middle height with a lovely figure, in a plain white dress trimmed with pink ribbons. She held a loaf of dark bread and was cutting slices for the little ones around her, each according to its age and appetite, handing them out with such grace and affection, every child waiting its turn with hands outstretched and shouting out its thanks. Some ran off at once with their supper, while the gentler ones walked out to the gate to look at the strangers and the carriage that was to carry their Charlotte away. "Do forgive me for making you come in for me, and for keeping the ladies waiting," she said. "What with dressing and arranging a few household things before I go out, I forgot to give the children their supper, and they won't take it from anyone but me." I made some empty compliment, but my whole soul was lost in her bearing, her voice, her way of moving, and I had barely collected myself when she darted into her room for her gloves and fan. The children eyed me from a little way off, and I went over to the youngest, the most delightful little creature. He drew back, and just then Charlotte came in and said, "Louis, give your cousin your hand." The little fellow did so readily, and I couldn't help giving him a hearty kiss in spite of his runny nose. "Cousin?" I said to Charlotte as I handed her down. "Do you think I deserve the good fortune of being related to you?" "Oh," she answered with an easy smile, "I have such a crowd of cousins that I'd be sorry to think you the least deserving of them." As she left she asked her next sister, Sophy, a girl of about eleven, to keep a close eye on the children and to say goodbye to their father for her when he got back from his ride. She told the little ones to mind their sister Sophy as if she were Charlotte herself, and some of them promised they would; but one fair-haired little girl of about six looked unhappy and said, "But Sophy isn't you, Charlotte, and we like you best." The two eldest boys had scrambled up onto the carriage, and at my request she let them ride a little way with us through the wood, on their promise to sit quite still and hold on tight.

englishChanges.before: When I walk out to Walheim at sunrise and there in the garden pick my own peas for dinner, and sit down to shell them while I read my Homer between handfuls; when I choose a pot in the little kitchen, cut myself a pat of butter, set my peas on the fire, cover them, and sit by to give them a stir now and then — I can feel so vividly how Penelope's overbearing suitors slaughtered and carved and roasted their own oxen and swine. Nothing fills me with so quiet and true a sense of happiness as these touches of patriarchal life, which, thank heaven, I can weave into my own without affectation. How glad I am that my heart can feel the simple, harmless joy of a man who brings to his table a cabbage he grew himself, and who in that one moment relives not just the cabbage but all the good days — the fine morning he planted it, the soft evenings he watered it, the pleasure he took in watching it grow — all of it together again.

Nothing fills me with so quiet and true a sense of happiness as these touches of patriarchal life, which, thank heaven, I can weave into my own without affectation. How glad I am that my heart can feel the simple, harmless joy of a man who brings to his table a cabbage he grew himself, and who in that one moment relives not just the cabbage but all the good days — the fine morning he planted it, the soft evenings he watered it, the pleasure he took in watching it grow — all of it together again.

englishChanges.before: I don't think I've told you yet what happened on the drive home from the ball — and I haven't time now either. It was the most glorious sunrise: the dripping wood, the freshened country all around. Our companions had dozed off. Charlotte asked whether I didn't want to sleep too, and begged me not to stay awake on her account. "As long as I can see those eyes open," I said, looking straight at her, "there's no danger of my falling asleep." We both stayed awake right to her door. The maid let us in softly and assured her, in answer to her questions, that her father and the children were well and still asleep. I left her, asking leave to call on her later that same day. She gave it, and I went; and since then sun, moon, and stars may go about their business as they please — I don't know whether it's day or night, and the whole world has melted away around me.

englishChanges.before: The comfort Charlotte can bring to a sick friend, I feel in my own heart, which suffers more from being apart from her than many a poor soul wasting away in bed. She's spending a few days in town with a worthy woman whom the doctors have given up, and who wants Charlotte near her at the end. Last week I went with her to visit the vicar of St—, a little village up in the hills about a league from here. We got there around four; Charlotte had brought her little sister along. As we came into the vicarage yard we found the good old man sitting on a bench by the door under the shade of two big walnut trees. At the sight of Charlotte he seemed to come to life, forgot his stick, and made to get up and walk toward her. She ran to him and made him sit down again, took a seat beside him, passed on a great many messages from her father, and then scooped up his youngest, an ugly, grubby little thing, the darling of his old age, and kissed it. I wish you could have seen how she gave herself to that old man — raising her voice for his deafness, telling him of strong young people carried off without warning, praising the waters at Carlsbad, approving his plan to spend the coming summer there, telling him he looked better and stronger than the last time she saw him. I, meanwhile, paid my respects to his wife. The old man grew quite cheerful, and since I couldn't help admiring the fine walnut trees that shaded us so pleasantly, he began, with a little effort, to tell us their story. "The older one," he said, "we don't know who planted — some say this parson, some that. But the younger one behind us is exactly my wife's age: fifty next October. Her father planted it the morning of the day she was born that evening. He was my predecessor here, and there's no telling how he loved that tree — and it's just as dear to me. My wife was sitting under it on a beam, knitting, when I first walked into this yard, a poor student, twenty-seven years ago." Charlotte asked after his daughter, and he said she'd gone out to the meadows with Herr Schmidt to see the haymakers, and then went on with his story: how his predecessor had taken a liking to him, and the daughter too, and how he'd become first the man's curate and then his successor. He'd barely finished when the daughter came back through the garden with this Herr Schmidt. She gave Charlotte a warm welcome, and I'll admit I rather liked her — a lively, good-natured brunette, the sort who could keep you amused for a while in the country. Her suitor (for that's plainly what Schmidt was) was a polite but reserved fellow who wouldn't join our talk however hard Charlotte tried to draw him out. What annoyed me most was seeing in his face that it was temper, not dullness, that kept him silent. This came out clearly later: when we set off on a walk and Frederica fell in beside Charlotte, and so beside me, the man's face, naturally rather dark, grew so black and sullen that Charlotte had to pluck my sleeve and warn me I was paying Frederica too much attention. Now nothing in the world vexes me more than to see people torment one another — above all when the young, in the very flower of life, in the very season for joy, throw away their few bright days on quarrels, and only see what they've done when it's too late to mend it. It weighed on me, and that evening, back at the vicarage and sitting round the table over our bread and milk, when the talk turned to the joys and sorrows of the world, I couldn't help laying into ill-humor. "We're forever complaining," I said, "that good days are so few and bad days so many — and usually with little reason. If our hearts were always open to take in the good that heaven sends us, we'd have the strength to bear the bad when it comes." "But we can't command our moods," said the vicar's wife. "So much depends on the body; when you're out of sorts physically, nothing feels right." "Granted," I said, "but then let's treat it as an illness and ask whether there isn't a cure."

englishChanges.before: At those words the memory of just such a scene I'd once stood through broke over me with full force. I pressed my handkerchief to my eyes and hurried out of the room, and only came back to myself at Charlotte's voice calling that it was time to go home. And how she scolded me on the way, so tenderly, for taking everything too much to heart — that it would be the ruin of me, that I must spare myself! Oh my angel — for your sake I will.
englishChanges.after: At those words the memory of just such a scene I'd once stood through broke over me with full force. I pressed my handkerchief to my eyes and hurried out of the room, and only came back to myself at Charlotte's voice calling that it was time to go home. And how she scolded me on the way, so tenderly, for taking everything too much to heart — that it would be the ruin of me, that I must spare myself! Oh, that angel! For your sake I must live!
englishChanges.reason: Restore primary German Um deinetwillen muss ich leben, decisive must-live declaration weakened in English intermediate.

englishChanges.before: The affection, the simplicity in the way she said it carried me away so that I couldn't find any way to show what I felt but to snatch the child up and kiss her warmly — at which she screamed and burst into tears. "You shouldn't have done that," said Charlotte. I stood there at a loss. "Come, Jane," she went on, taking her by the hand and leading her down the steps, "never mind — quick, wash it off in the fresh water, quick." I stood watching as the little thing scrubbed away at her cheeks with her wet hands, certain that the miraculous water would rinse off every trace of contamination from my ugly stubble; and though Charlotte said that was enough, she kept scrubbing with all her might, as if too much were safer than too little. I tell you, Wilhelm, I never stood at a baptism with more reverence; and when Charlotte came back up I could have bowed down before her as before a prophet who had washed away a nation's sins.
englishChanges.after: The affection, the simplicity in the way she said it carried me away so that I couldn't find any way to show what I felt but to snatch the child up and kiss her warmly — at which she screamed and burst into tears. "You shouldn't have done that," said Charlotte. I stood there at a loss. "Come, Jane," she went on, taking her by the hand and leading her down the steps, "never mind — quick, wash it off in the fresh water, quick." I stood watching as the little thing scrubbed away at her cheeks with her wet hands, certain that the miraculous water would rinse away every impurity and save her from the disgrace of growing an ugly beard; and though Charlotte said that was enough, she kept scrubbing with all her might, as if too much were safer than too little. I tell you, Wilhelm, I never stood at a baptism with more reverence; and when Charlotte came back up I could have bowed down before her as before a prophet who had washed away a nation's sins.
englishChanges.reason: German primary hässlichen Bart zu kriegen: child fears growing a beard, not contamination from his stubble.

englishChanges.before: Madame M— is very ill. I pray she'll recover, because Charlotte suffers along with her. I see Charlotte now and then at my friend's house, and today she told me the strangest thing. Old M— is a grasping, tight-fisted fellow who has long pinched and plagued the poor woman, though she's borne it patiently. A few days ago, when the doctor told us there was no hope for her, she sent for her husband — Charlotte was in the room — and said to him: "I have something to confess that could cause trouble and confusion after I'm gone. I've kept your house as thriftily and carefully as I could all these years — but you'll have to forgive me for cheating you for thirty of them. When we were first married you set aside a small sum for the kitchen and the other household needs. As our household grew and our means with it, I could never get you to raise the weekly housekeeping to match; you know that even when our needs were greatest you insisted I run everything on seven florins a week. I took the money without a word and made up the difference each week out of the cash box, since no one would suspect the mistress of robbing the till. I've wasted nothing, and I could have gone to meet my Maker without saying any of this — except that whoever takes over the house after me won't know how to manage, and you'll keep insisting that your first wife got by on the same sum."
englishChanges.after: Madame M— is very ill. I pray she'll recover, because I share Charlotte's suffering. I see Charlotte now and then at my friend's house, and today she told me the strangest thing. Old M— is a grasping, tight-fisted fellow who has long pinched and plagued the poor woman, though she has always found a way to manage. A few days ago, when the doctor told us there was no hope for her, she sent for her husband — Charlotte was in the room — and said to him: "I have something to confess that could cause trouble and confusion after I'm gone. I've kept your house as thriftily and carefully as I could all these years — but you'll have to forgive me for cheating you for thirty of them. When we were first married you set aside a small sum for the kitchen and the other household needs. As our household and business grew, I could never get you to raise the weekly housekeeping to match; you know that even when our needs were greatest you insisted I run everything on seven florins a week. I took the money without a word and made up the difference each week out of the takings, since no one would suspect the mistress of robbing the till. I've wasted nothing, and I could have gone to meet my Maker without saying any of this — except that whoever takes over the house after me won't know how to manage, and you'll keep insisting that your first wife got by on the same sum."
englishChanges.reason: German: weil ich mit Lotten dulde; wife found ways to manage; growing business and weekly takings, not passive patience.

englishChanges.before: Not a word that's ever been said about the old magic of music seems unlikely to me now. How that simple song takes hold of me! And how well she knows when to play it — often just when I feel like putting a bullet through my head. The darkness and madness in me scatter, and I breathe more freely again.
englishChanges.after: Not a word that's ever been said about the magical power of ancient music seems unlikely to me now. How that simple song takes hold of me! And how well she knows when to play it — often just when I feel like putting a bullet through my head. The darkness and madness in me scatter, and I breathe more freely again.
englishChanges.reason: German der alten Musik refers to music of antiquity, not an old magic belonging to music.

englishChanges.before: Many a time I've resolved not to see her so often. But who could keep such a vow! Every day I give in to the temptation, swearing faithfully that tomorrow, for once, I'll stay away — and when tomorrow comes I find some irresistible reason all over again, and before I know how, I'm with her. Either she's said the evening before, "You'll come tomorrow, won't you?" — and who could stay away after that? — or she gives me an errand, and I find it only proper to bring her the answer myself; or the day is too fine, and I walk out to Walheim, and once I'm there it's only half a league more to her — and I'm too close to the spell not to be drawn in, and there I am with her again. My grandmother used to tell us a tale of a magnetic mountain: any ship that sailed too near it was stripped of all its iron in an instant, the nails flying off to the mountain, and the poor sailors went down among the collapsing planks.

My grandmother used to tell us a tale of a magnetic mountain: any ship that sailed too near it was stripped of all its iron in an instant, the nails flying off to the mountain, and the poor sailors went down among the collapsing planks.
englishChanges.reason: German halbe Stunde: half-hour walking distance, not half a league.

englishChanges.before: He tells me about her good mother — how on her deathbed she handed over her house and children to Charlotte, and Charlotte herself to him; how from that day a new spirit had filled the girl, how in her care and worry over the household she became a true mother to them, how not one moment of her time passed without active love and work, and yet her cheerfulness and her light heart never left her. I walk along beside him, picking flowers by the path, weaving them carefully into a little wreath, and then — throwing it into the stream as it runs by, watching it bob gently away downstream. I don't know whether I told you that Albert is to stay here; he's been given a post at court with a good salary, and stands high in favor there. In matters of business I've met few people so orderly and exact.
englishChanges.after: He tells me about her good mother — how on her deathbed she handed over her house and children to Charlotte, and Charlotte herself to him; how from that day a new spirit had filled the girl, how in her care and worry over the household she became a true mother to them, how not one moment of her time passed without active love and work, and yet her cheerfulness and her light heart never left her. I walk along beside him, picking flowers by the path, arranging them carefully into a bouquet, and then — throwing them into the stream as it runs by, watching them float gently away downstream. I don't know whether I told you that Albert is to stay here; he will be given a post with a good income from the court, and stands high in favor there. In matters of business I've met few people so orderly and exact.
englishChanges.reason: German Strauß and original English nosegay mean bouquet, not wreath. German erhalten wird makes appointment prospective.

englishChanges.before: Albert is certainly the best fellow alive. I had a strange scene with him yesterday. I'd gone to take my leave, since the whim took me to ride up into these hills, from which I'm writing to you now. As I was pacing his room my eye fell on his pistols. "Lend me the pistols," I said, "for the journey." "Gladly," he said, "if you'll take the trouble to load them; they only hang there for show." I took one down, and he went on, "Ever since my caution played me such a nasty trick, I won't have anything more to do with the things." I was curious to hear the story. "I was staying about three months," he said, "at a friend's place in the country. I had a pair of unloaded pocket-pistols, and slept easy. One rainy afternoon, sitting about with nothing to do, it came into my head — I don't know how — that we might be attacked, that we might need the pistols, that — well, you know how it goes when one has nothing better to do. I handed them to the servant to clean and load. He was fooling with the maid, trying to scare her, and somehow — God knows how — the gun went off, the ramrod still down the barrel, and drove it into the ball of her right thumb and smashed it. So I had her wailing to put up with and the surgeon's bill to pay into the bargain, and ever since I've kept my weapons unloaded. My dear fellow, what good is caution? You can't learn every danger in advance. To be sure —" Now, you must know, I can get along with a man right up to his "to be sure"; for surely it goes without saying that every general rule has its exceptions. But the man is so terribly careful that the moment he thinks he's said something a bit too rash, too sweeping, only half true, he won't stop qualifying and trimming and whittling away until in the end there's nothing left of it at all. And on this occasion he got so deep into the text that I stopped listening to him altogether and fell to brooding, and with one sudden motion I pressed the muzzle of the pistol to my forehead, above the right eye. "Good God," cried Albert, pulling the pistol down, "what is this?" "It isn't loaded," I said. "Even so — what do you mean by it?" he snapped. "I can't imagine how a man could be foolish enough to shoot himself; the very thought disgusts me."

I handed them to the servant to clean and load. He was fooling with the girls, trying to scare them, and somehow — God knows how — the gun went off, the ramrod still down the barrel, and drove it into the ball of her right thumb and smashed it. So I had her wailing to put up with and the surgeon's bill to pay into the bargain, and ever since I've kept my weapons unloaded. My dear fellow, what good is caution? You can't learn every danger in advance. To be sure —" Now, you must know, I am very fond of him, apart from his "to be sure"; for surely it goes without saying that every general rule has its exceptions. But the man is so terribly careful that the moment he thinks he's said something a bit too rash, too sweeping, only half true, he won't stop qualifying and trimming and whittling away until in the end there's nothing left of it at all. And on this occasion he went so deeply into the subject that I stopped listening to him altogether and fell to brooding, and with one sudden motion I pressed the muzzle of the pistol to my forehead, above the right eye. "Good God," cried Albert, pulling the pistol down, "what is this?" "It isn't loaded," I said. "Even so — what do you mean by it?" he snapped. "I can't imagine how a man could be foolish enough to shoot himself; the very thought disgusts me."
englishChanges.reason: German girls plural, personal affection for Albert, idiomatic treatment of tief in Text.

englishChanges.before: "But you'll grant me," said Albert, "that certain acts are wicked, whatever the motive behind them." I shrugged and let it pass.
englishChanges.after: "But you'll grant me," said Albert, "that certain acts are wicked, whatever the motive behind them." I shrugged and agreed.
englishChanges.reason: German gab's ihm zu and original granted it: actual concession, not merely letting it pass.

englishChanges.before: "Oh, you reasonable people!" I cried, smiling. "Passion! Drunkenness! Madness! There you stand, so cool, so unconcerned, you moral men — scolding the drunkard, loathing the madman, passing by on the other side like the Levite, and thanking God like the Pharisee that he hasn't made you as one of them. I've been drunk more than once, my passions have never been far from madness, and I'm not ashamed of either; for I've learned, in my own way, that all extraordinary men who ever did something great, something that seemed impossible, have always been cried down as drunk or mad. And in ordinary life too it's unbearable to hear it said of nearly anyone who does a halfway free, noble, unexpected thing: the man is drunk, he's a fool! Shame on you sober ones, shame on you sages!"
englishChanges.after: "Oh, you reasonable people!" I cried, smiling. "Passion! Drunkenness! Madness! There you stand, so cool, so unconcerned, you moral men — scolding the drunkard, loathing the madman, passing by on the other side like the priest, and thanking God like the Pharisee that he hasn't made you as one of them. I've been drunk more than once, my passions have never been far from madness, and I regret neither; for I've learned, in my own way, that all extraordinary men who ever did something great, something that seemed impossible, have always been cried down as drunk or mad. And in ordinary life too it's unbearable to hear it said of nearly anyone who does a halfway free, noble, unexpected thing: the man is drunk, he's a fool! Shame on you sober ones, shame on you sages!"
englishChanges.reason: German Priester and reut correct inherited English allusion and regret/shame distinction.

englishChanges.before: "Paradoxical! Quite paradoxical!" Albert exclaimed. "Not so much as you think," I replied. "You'll admit we call a sickness mortal when nature is so hard hit, her forces so far spent, that she can't pull herself together again, can't by any lucky turn set the ordinary course of life going once more."
englishChanges.after: "Paradoxical! Quite paradoxical!" Albert exclaimed. "Not so much as you think," I replied. "You'll admit we call a sickness mortal when nature is so hard hit, her forces partly spent and partly put out of action, that she can't pull herself together again, can't by any lucky turn set the ordinary course of life going once more."
englishChanges.reason: Restore German two separate effects: exhausted powers and disabled powers.

englishChanges.before: "Woe to the man who can look on and say, 'The foolish girl! If she'd only waited, if she'd only let time do its work, the despair would have died down, and some other man would have turned up to comfort her.' That's as good as saying, 'The fool! to die of a fever! If he'd only waited till his strength came back, his blood settled, the turmoil in it died away — all would have gone well, and he'd be alive to this day!'"
englishChanges.after: "Woe to the man who can look on and say, 'The foolish girl! If she'd only waited, if she'd only let time do its work, the despair would have died down, and some other man would have turned up to comfort her.' That's as good as saying, 'The fool! to die of a fever! If he'd only waited till his strength came back, his bodily humours improved, and the turmoil in his blood died away — all would have gone well, and he'd be alive to this day!'"
englishChanges.reason: Restore German Säfte, historical humoral medicine reference omitted from English intermediate.

englishChanges.before: Wretch that I am! Aren't you a fool? Aren't you fooling yourself? What's to come of this raging, endless passion? I have no prayers left but to her; no shape comes before my imagination but hers; I see nothing in all the world around me except in relation to her. And that gives me many a happy hour — until I have to tear myself away from her again! Ah, Wilhelm, what my heart so often drives me to! When I've sat with her two or three hours and feasted on her form, her bearing, the heavenly expression of her words, and little by little all my senses are wound to the highest pitch, my eyes darken, I can scarcely hear, something grips me by the throat like a murderer, and then my wild heart tries to give my senses air and only deepens their confusion — Wilhelm, often I hardly know whether I'm in the world at all! And — unless the sadness sometimes gets the upper hand and Charlotte allows me the wretched comfort of weeping out my anguish over her hand — I have to get away, out, and I roam far over the fields; my joy then is to climb a steep hill, to break a path through a trackless wood where the thorns gash me and the briars tear me! Then I feel a little better. A little! And when I sometimes lie down on the way, dead with weariness and thirst, sometimes deep in the night, with the full moon high above me, and in the lonely wood sit myself on a crooked tree to give my torn feet some relief, and then doze off in the faint light in an exhausted calm! O Wilhelm! the lonely cell, the hair shirt and the belt of thorns would be balm to the soul I pant for. Adieu! I see no end to this misery but the grave.

englishChanges.reason: German Labsale, nach denen meine Seele schmachtet: the soul longs for comforts, not a narrator longing for a soul.

englishChanges.before: I'd spent maybe half an hour given over to the parting and meeting thoughts of death and the life beyond, when I heard them coming up to the terrace. I ran to meet them, took her hand with a shiver, and kissed it. We'd just reached the top when the moon came up behind the bushy hill; we talked of all sorts of things and came, without noticing, nearer the gloomy little clearing. Charlotte stepped in and sat down, Albert beside her, and I too — though my restlessness wouldn't let me sit for long; I got up, stood before her, paced back and forth, sat down again: it was an anxious state. She drew our notice to the lovely play of the moonlight, which at the end of the wall of beeches lit up the whole terrace before us — a glorious sight, all the more striking because deep darkness hemmed us in on every side. We fell silent, and after a while she said, "I never walk in the moonlight, never, without my dead coming to meet me, without the feeling of death, of what is to come, sweeping over me. We shall live again!" she went on, in the voice of the most glorious feeling; "but, Werther, shall we find one another again? know one another again? What do you sense? What do you say?"

Charlotte stepped in and sat down, Albert beside her, and I too — though my restlessness wouldn't let me sit for long; I got up, stood before her, paced back and forth, sat down again: it was an anxious state. She drew our notice to the lovely play of the moonlight, which at the end of the wall of beeches lit up the whole terrace before us — a glorious sight, all the more striking because deep darkness hemmed us in on every side. We fell silent, and after a while she said, "I never walk in the moonlight, never, without my dead coming to meet me, without the feeling of death, of what is to come, sweeping over me. We shall live again!" she went on, in the voice of the most glorious feeling; "but, Werther, shall we find one another again? know one another again? What do you sense? What do you say?"

englishChanges.before: And the glittering misery, the boredom, among the dreary people thrown together here! Their hunger for rank, the way they watch and lie in wait for the least step ahead of one another; the pettiest, most wretched passions, utterly naked. There's a woman, for instance, who bends everyone's ear about her noble birth and her lands, so that any stranger must think her a fool, puffed up over the bit of nobility and the name of her estate — when in fact she's nothing more than the daughter of a local clerk. You see, I can't make sense of a race of people who debase themselves so shamelessly.

englishChanges.before: Count O— likes me, singles me out — you know that, I've told you a hundred times. Yesterday I dined with him, on the very day his grand company of lords and ladies gathers at his house in the evening, which I never gave a thought to, and it never struck me that we underlings don't belong there. Good. I dine with the count, and after dinner we walk up and down the great hall; I talk with him, with Colonel B— who joins us, and so the hour for the party comes on. God knows, I'm thinking of nothing. In sweeps the more-than-gracious Lady von S— with her lord and her well-hatched little gosling of a daughter, with her flat chest and trim little waist; in passing they make their high-born eyes and nostrils at me in the old approved style. And since I heartily detest the whole tribe, I was just about to take my leave, only waiting for the count to be free of their wretched chatter, when my Miss B— came in. As my heart always lifts a little at the sight of her, I stayed on, stood behind her chair, and only after a while noticed that she was talking to me with less than her usual openness, a little flustered. It struck me. Is she like all the rest? I thought, and was stung, and meant to go — and yet stayed, because I wanted to excuse her, and didn't believe it, and still hoped for a kind word from her, and — whatever you like. Meanwhile the room filled up. Baron F— in a whole wardrobe inherited from the coronation of Francis I; the court councillor R—, with his deaf wife; the shabbily turned-out J—, patching the gaps of his old-fashioned coat with new bits. They came in droves, and I talked with a few of my acquaintances, who were all very curt. I was thinking — and only had eyes for my Miss B—. I didn't notice the women whispering at the far end of the room, that it spread to the men, that Frau von S— spoke to the count (Miss B— told me all this afterward), until at last the count came up to me and drew me over to a window. "You know our odd ways," he said. "The company, I notice, is displeased to see you here. I wouldn't for the world —" "Your Excellency," I broke in, "I beg your pardon a thousand times; I should have thought of it sooner, and I know you'll forgive me this inconsistency. I meant to take my leave a while ago; an evil genius held me back," I added with a smile, and bowed. The count pressed my hand with a feeling that said everything. I slipped quietly out of the grand company, got into a carriage, and drove to M—, to watch the sunset from the hill there and read in my Homer the glorious canto where Ulysses is entertained by the noble swineherd. That was good.

englishChanges.before: In the evening I came back to supper. Only a few were still in the room, dicing in a corner with the cloth turned back. Then the good A— came in, laid down his hat when he saw me, came up to me and said softly, "You've had trouble?" "I?" I said. "The count sent you out of the party." "The devil take the party," I said. "I was glad to get into the open air." "Good," he said, "that you take it lightly. Only it vexes me that it's already all over the place." Now the thing began to gnaw at me. Everyone who came to table and looked at me — I imagined it was because of that. It made my blood boil.
